You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Viktor

Viktor was seventy-six when he walked into the clinic on a Tuesday morning in November, moving with the careful deliberation of a man who no longer fully trusted his own legs. He had spent forty-three years managing hotels—the Grandview in downtown Denver, the Riverside in Aspen, most recently a boutique property near Boulder—and had built a reputation for precision and unflappable composure. That composure had fractured on a March afternoon two years ago when a contractor's crew had ruptured a chemical line in the basement mechanical room while Viktor was conducting his routine inspection. The acrid smell hit him first—a choking, metallic burn that coated the back of his throat—followed by the sound of liquid hissing across concrete. He had stumbled backward, his lungs seizing, vision swimming, and in those moments before he reached the stairs, he had been certain he was dying. The hospital confirmed chemical pneumonitis, a course of steroids, and a prognosis of full recovery. But recovery, Viktor had come to understand, was not the same as healing.

The first months had been manageable. He returned to work in May, determined to reclaim his routine. But by July, something had shifted. Unexpected noises—a car backfiring, a door slamming, even the hiss of the espresso machine in the hotel lobby—would send his heart into a gallop, his palms slick with sweat. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his to command, that it had become an adversary, erupting in panic at moments when his rational mind insisted there was no danger. The knowledge that he could not control these reactions, that his own physiology had turned traitor, had settled into a deep, immobilizing dread. This persistent sense of threat—that his body might betray him again without warning, that danger could arrive unannounced—quietly confirmed the conviction that had taken root: the world was fundamentally unsafe, and he was powerless to protect himself. He was certain now that he could not stop bad things from happening—that the world was fundamentally unsafe and his body would betray him again without warning. This conviction seeped into every room of his apartment. Even at home, behind locked doors, he felt exposed, scanning for threats, his shoulders rigid, his breath shallow. He had begun to believe that safety existed in only a handful of places: his bedroom with the curtains drawn, his therapist's office, the car with the windows up. Everywhere else felt permeable, hostile.

The memories themselves were fragmented and strange. Sometimes Viktor would be standing in his kitchen, reaching for a coffee mug, when he would be flooded with the full emotional intensity of that March afternoon—the terror, the suffocation, the conviction that he was dying—but without any clear image, as though the fear had detached from its source and become free-floating. Other times, a particular smell would surface: not the chemical itself, but something close enough—cleaning solution, a stranger's cologne, even the mineral scent of the hotel's humidifier—and suddenly he could taste that acrid burn, could feel his lungs constricting, the memory arriving in pieces that never quite assembled into a coherent narrative. These fragmentary recollections had begun to feel like proof that he was losing his mind. The fear that he was "going crazy" had become as present as the fear of the chemical itself, and Viktor had developed a habit of monitoring his own thoughts constantly, watching for signs of deterioration, checking whether his thinking was still rational. This vigilance exhausted him but felt necessary, a kind of mental sentry duty.

To manage the intrusions, Viktor had turned to distraction. He kept the television on almost constantly now, the volume loud enough to drown out any unexpected sound from the street or hallway. Music played in his car during the short drives he still permitted himself. The noise created a kind of buffer, a wall between himself and the unpredictable world, and as long as the sound continued, he could maintain a fragile sense of control. He had learned that if he kept the television loud enough, if he stayed in motion, the fragmentary recollections could not find their footing—but the moment the noise stopped, the memories were there again, waiting. But the distraction fed back into his sense of helplessness: he recognized that he needed the noise to feel safe, and that dependency itself became evidence that he was unraveling, that he could no longer manage his own mind. His work had suffered. He had taken medical leave in September, ostensibly temporary, but the thought of returning to the hotel—of being in that building, of hearing the mechanical systems hum, of navigating the basement where the exposure had occurred—was impossible. He had avoided the site entirely, unable even to drive past it. His colleagues had stopped calling. His ex-wife, with whom he had maintained cordial contact for years, had become distant after he cancelled three consecutive dinner invitations, unable to explain why he could not leave his apartment in the evening.

What had finally brought Viktor to seek help was a moment of clarity that felt more like capitulation. He was sitting in his darkened bedroom, the television murmuring, when he realized he could not remember the last time he had felt safe. Not just safe—present. The thought that he might spend the remainder of his life in this small, shrinking space, waiting for disaster, had broken something open. He arrived at the clinic asking a single question: whether there was any way to trust his body again, or whether he would have to learn to live as a prisoner of its betrayals. To stop the memories coming at night, Viktor started keeping the television on constantly, the noise a barrier between himself and the intrusions that seemed to arrive whenever silence gave them room to breathe.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: Negative Appraisals → Threat: While negative appraisals appear throughout (e.g., 'world was fundamentally unsafe,' 'body would betray him'), and threat appears as a persistent sense of danger, no paragraph explicitly conveys that the negative appraisals themselves drive or lead to the threat perception; the threat is presented as arising from the body's unpredictable reactions rather than from the appraisals.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: Although intrusive memories are described extensively and maladaptive strategies (constant television, distraction, avoidance) are detailed, no paragraph directly conveys that the memories themselves drive Viktor to adopt these strategies; instead, the strategies are framed as responses to threat and intrusions more generally.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Memory: Threat → Memory: The vignette describes threat perception and memories as coexisting features but does not establish a causal pathway where the sense of threat (perceived danger, body betrayal) leads to or triggers the intrusive memories; the relationship is presented as correlational rather than directional.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He was certain now that he could not stop bad things from happening—that the world was fundamentally unsafe and his body would betray him again without warning. This conviction seeped into every room of his apartment.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Having decided that the world was fundamentally unsafe and his body could not be trusted, Viktor walked through his apartment already braced for danger—the threat arrived with him before anything had happened, a shadow cast by his own certainty of vulnerability.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Other times, a particular smell would surface: not the chemical itself, but something close enough—cleaning solution, a stranger's cologne, even the mineral scent of the hotel's humidifier—and suddenly he could taste that acrid burn, could feel his lungs constricting, the memory arriving in pieces that never quite assembled into a coherent narrative.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
These fragmentary recollections had begun to feel intolerable, and Viktor had learned that if he kept the television on loud enough, if he filled every moment with noise and distraction, the memories could not find their footing—silence was the enemy, and so he had become dependent on constant sound to keep them at bay.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This persistent sense of threat—that his body might betray him again without warning, that danger could arrive unannounced—quietly confirmed the conviction that had taken root: the world was fundamentally unsafe, and he was powerless to protect himself.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
On nights when the threat felt highest, when his body seemed most poised to betray him, the memory was hardest to keep at bay—it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome, pulled out of him by the adrenaline, fully formed, as though his vigilance had summoned it.
<<<END>>>
